---
title: "xenium_nb: sample summary"
subtitle: "Clusters and centroid correlation, one sample per section"
# Pin the kernel by name, as cluster_report.qmd does. Apptainer bind-mounts $HOME, so
# kernelspecs from ~/.local/share/jupyter/kernels shadow the container's own — quarto's
# default "python3" then resolves to a host env missing the pipeline's packages, and
# every cell fails at import under `error: true` while the render still exits 0.
jupyter: python_spatial
format:
  pptx:
    reference-doc: ouhsc_ppt_template.pptx
    # `#` becomes a Section Header slide, `##` a Title-and-Content slide. Without
    # this pandoc infers the level from the headings present, so adding the first
    # `#` would silently demote every `##` to a bullet.
    slide-level: 2
execute:
  echo: false
  warning: false
  # Keep rendering when a cell raises: one sample's panel erroring leaves an error slide
  # in its own section instead of taking the whole deck down. The cost is that a
  # genuinely broken cell yields an error slide and an exit code of 0 — read the slides,
  # not just the exit status.
  error: true
---

```{python}
# | tags: [setup]
import gc
import logging
import traceback
import warnings
from pathlib import Path

import matplotlib.patheffects as patheffects
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import scanpy as sc
import spatialdata as sd
import spatialdata_plot  # noqa: F401 — registers the .pl accessor used by the zoom slides
import yaml
from IPython.display import display, Markdown
from matplotlib.colors import to_hex
from matplotlib.patches import Rectangle
from matplotlib.text import Text
from matplotlib_scalebar.scalebar import ScaleBar
from spatialdata.models import PointsModel
from spatialdata.transformations import get_transformation
from scipy.cluster.hierarchy import leaves_list, linkage
from scipy.spatial.distance import squareform

# Chatter from the zoom slides, suppressed by message rather than wholesale: each of these
# fires once per zoom, describes something the deck does deliberately, and would otherwise
# bury a message worth reading in a cohort-sized render. `warning: false` in the front
# matter keeps them off the SLIDES; this keeps them out of the render log too.
#
#   colormapping   render_points draws a categorical column, so cmap/norm do not apply.
#   points/query   bounding_box is told the object has points and may be slow. It is the
#                  crop we want, and a 200 µm window is small.
#   feature_key    marker_set is a pandas Categorical by the time PointsModel sees it,
#                  which is deliberate: the category order is what fixes the draw order.
#   z ignored      the points carry a z column and these plots are 2D.
warnings.filterwarnings("ignore", message="No data for colormapping provided")
warnings.filterwarnings("ignore", message="The object has `points` element")
logging.getLogger("spatialdata").setLevel(logging.ERROR)

# The reference template is 16:9 at 10 x 5.625in; leave room for a slide title.
FIGSIZE = (9.0, 4.3)

# Inches reserved beside the in-tissue plot for its cluster legend, which sits outside
# the axes and would otherwise be cropped by tight_layout.
SPATIAL_LEGEND_WIDTH = 1.2
# Fraction of the in-tissue axes the cell dots should cover, which sets their size. A
# fixed size cannot serve every section: at s=3 a 21k-cell strip reads well but a
# 32k-cell section is a solid mat, and at s=1 the strip is speckle.
SPATIAL_COVERAGE = 0.45

# Fraction of the embedding's own span left as margin around every UMAP panel, so the
# cells at the edge are not clipped by the axes. One value for all of them, since the
# panels are meant to be the same picture at different sizes.
UMAP_MARGIN = 0.04

# Raster resolution for every figure in the deck, set once here rather than per call.
# Matplotlib's default is 100, which is what made the text soft: these figures are 9in
# wide on a 10in slide, so a 7pt label is about ten pixels tall before PowerPoint scales
# it up. qc_report.qmd carries the full reasoning for the number — briefly, 400 covers a
# 4K screen at this figure width, 300 covers 1440p and print at 100%, 200 covers a 1080p
# projector and nothing above it.
#
# Only the dpi is set. This deck passes an explicit fontsize to nearly every text call
# already, so adopting qc_report's font rcParams as well would change only the handful of
# places that do not, and reshuffle layouts that were tuned against the current sizes.
#
# The cost is file size, and it is quadratic in the number: two samples at 400 dpi came to
# 67 MB, which a six-sample cohort extrapolates to ~200 MB. 200 dpi is a quarter of those
# pixels and was chosen on that trade — it still covers a 1080p projector, which is what
# these slides are actually shown on, and gives up only zooming in past 100%.
plt.rcParams.update({
    "figure.dpi": 200,
    "savefig.dpi": 200,
})

# Every clustered zarr is staged into this notebook's working directory by the Nextflow
# process, so globbing is the whole input contract — no params to pass or drift. These
# are cluster_sdata's zarrs, not create_sdata's: they carry the leiden_res_* columns,
# and their cells are already past the min_counts cut.
ZARRS = sorted(Path(".").glob("*.zarr"))
if not ZARRS:
    raise FileNotFoundError("No .zarr directories staged next to the notebook.")

# The resolution each sample's clusters are taken at unless its row in
# chosen_resolutions.csv says otherwise. A cohort-wide starting point, not a claim that
# 0.5 is right for any particular sample — the right resolution is a judgement made by
# reading cluster_report, and this is what the deck splits on until that judgement exists.
DEFAULT_RESOLUTION = 0.5

# The per-sample resolution table, staged flat beside the zarrs by the same
# staging-is-the-contract rule. Its rows are OVERRIDES on DEFAULT_RESOLUTION, not a
# required entry per sample: a cohort renders with no rows at all, and a sample gets its
# own resolution the moment one is written for it. Optional as a file too — if it is
# absent every sample simply takes the default.
RESOLUTIONS_CSV = Path("chosen_resolutions.csv")

# Hand-made cell type calls, staged flat beside the zarrs like the resolution table and
# optional in the same way: absent, every cell type falls back to its argmax cluster.
#
# One row per (sample, cell_type, cluster), because the relation is many-to-many in BOTH
# directions. One cell type over many clusters: a stroma-dominated section splits into
# several stromal clusters and they are all Stromal. One cluster under many cell types: a
# follicle sectioned whole is granulosa cells around an oocyte, and on ROI1_B both sets
# peak on the same cluster. A blank cluster means "not present in this sample", which is
# a real judgement and must survive rather than falling back to the argmax.
#
# Keyed on cluster_v2 — the ids the slides are labelled with, so a call can be written
# down from what is on screen. The cost is that v2 is derived from the dendrogram at
# render time: re-cluster, change resolution, or change the centroids and the ids
# repoint, so existing rows attach to different clusters without complaint. The deck
# warns when a row names a v2 id the sample does not have, which catches gross drift but
# not a silent renumbering. Re-derive the calls after re-clustering rather than trusting
# an old sheet. cluster_annotations.csv carries v1 alongside for exactly this reason.
CELL_TYPES_CSV = Path("cell_type_annotations.csv")

# Follicle marker sets, staged flat beside the zarrs by the same rule. Built by
# scripts/convert_ovary_reference.py from Sci Adv adm7506 Data S5, whose Granulosa,
# Oocyte and Theca sheets carry per-sample values rather than per-cell-type means — so
# these can only be SCORED, not correlated the way the major-type reference is.
#
# Required, not optional: unlike chosen_resolutions.csv, a missing file here would
# silently drop a whole section rather than fall back to a sensible default, and the
# follicle types are the ones the major-type reference cannot name at all.
MARKERS_YAML = Path("ovary_follicle_markers.yaml")

# Worst marker-quality score to keep, on the paper's own 1-5 scale: 1 established
# marker, 2 well annotated and biologically significant, 3 well annotated but not
# biologically significant, 4 poorly annotated gene, 5 poor marker based on comparisons
# across clusters.
#
# The asset carries every gene with its score and the filter happens HERE, so changing
# how conservative this is costs an edit to one line rather than a re-run of
# scripts/convert_ovary_reference.py over the source workbooks.
#
# Keeping everything is not a neutral default. Of the 19 theca markers on a 5K panel, 6
# are score 5 and 3 more are score 4 — more than half of what would be scored is flagged
# as bad by the people who assembled the list, which is the likeliest reason theca has
# never resolved anything on these samples. At 1 the sets are small but canonical: 10
# granulosa (AMH, FOXL2, FST, GREM1, HSD17B1...), 7 oocyte (FIGLA, LHX8, NLRP5, OOSP2,
# PADI6...) and 5 theca (CYP11A1, CYP17A1, DLK1, INSL3...) on that panel.
MARKER_MAX_SCORE = 1

# Scores are relative, not absolute. sc.tl.score_genes subtracts the mean of a
# reference set of similarly-expressed genes, so a score near zero means "no different
# from background", values are comparable only ACROSS cells within a sample, and no
# threshold separates positive from negative. A cluster scoring highest for a set is
# evidence; a merely positive score is not.
_scored_markers = yaml.safe_load(MARKERS_YAML.read_text()) if MARKERS_YAML.exists() else {}
if not _scored_markers:
    raise FileNotFoundError(f"{MARKERS_YAML} not staged beside the notebook.")
# An unscored gene (null in the asset) is dropped rather than kept: the paper scored
# every marker it published, so a missing score means the sheet changed shape and the
# safe reading is not to trust the gene.
MARKER_SETS = {
    name: sorted(gene for gene, score in genes.items()
                 if score is not None and score <= MARKER_MAX_SCORE)
    for name, genes in _scored_markers.items()
}

# The major cell-type reference: genes x cell type mean expression, built by
# scripts/convert_ovary_reference.py from Sci Adv adm7506 Data S6 and staged flat under
# this name. Cluster centroids are correlated against its columns to name them.
REFERENCE_CSV = Path("ovary_reference_major.csv.gz")
if not REFERENCE_CSV.exists():
    raise FileNotFoundError(f"{REFERENCE_CSV} not staged beside the notebook.")
REFERENCE = pd.read_csv(REFERENCE_CSV, index_col=0)

# The correlation runs over every gene the sample and the reference share, with no
# selection beyond that intersection. Simplicity is the point: the gene set is then a
# property of the panel and the reference rather than a choice this deck makes, and there
# is no parameter to tune or asset to keep in step.
#
# The cost is real and worth knowing. Most genes do not discriminate between these four
# types, so centroids correlate with every column at ~0.8 and the margin between the best
# match and the runner-up is thin: measured on the two test ROIs, 0.096 and 0.099 against
# 0.23-0.25 for a set restricted to the paper's own type-specific genes, and Endothelial
# and Pericyte fall on the same cluster where the restricted set separates all four. A
# type the reference does not contain still gets a confident-looking winner.

# The hand-curated oocyte list, staged flat beside the zarrs under this fixed name. One
# row per putative oocyte with the stage a curator assigned it, how confident they were,
# and its segmented area.
#
# Cells are matched to a sample by whether their cell_id is in that sample's obs_names,
# NOT by the sheet's Donor.ROI column. The column names the whole slide (ROI1) while a
# sample here is a crop of it (ROI1_A), so a name join finds nothing — while id
# membership scopes to the crop for free, and keeps working for whole-slide samples.
OOCYTES_CSV = Path("curated_oocytes.csv")

# Developmental order, which is the order the zoom slides run in — the section reads as a
# series rather than as whatever order the sheet happens to hold. Labels outside this list
# still get a slide, after these, so a curator adding a stage does not lose it silently.
OOCYTE_STAGE_ORDER = ["primordial", "early transitioning", "transitioning",
                      "late transitioning", "primary", "secondary"]

# Dropped rather than given a slide: "other" names no stage, and it is the single largest
# label in the sheet (186 of 542 across the six ROIs), so it would take a slide per sample
# to say nothing about development. The rows stay in the sheet — this only skips them here.
OOCYTE_STAGE_EXCLUDE = {"other"}

# Worst-to-best ordering of the curator's own confidence, used to pick which oocyte
# represents a stage. Ranked rather than filtered: a stage whose only cells are poor still
# gets its slide, captioned with that quality, because "the only primary oocyte in this
# section is a poor one" is itself worth seeing. An unrecognised value sorts last.
OOCYTE_QUALITY_RANK = {"good": 0, "okay": 1, "poor": 2, "terrible": 3}

# Half-width of the zoom window, in µm. The window is a SQUARE: the crop is a bounding
# box of +/- this many µm in x and y around the cell centre, so the slides describe it as
# 2 x this on a side. obsm["spatial"] is in µm for a Xenium read
# (verified: the test crops span exactly the 2000x700 and 1000x2200 boxes
# downsample_xenium_region was given). 100 µm puts a ~30 µm oocyte at about a seventh of
# the window and still shows the follicle's surroundings, which is what says whether the
# cluster tracks the oocyte or the whole follicle. At ~0.015 cells/µm² the window holds
# roughly 600 cells.
ZOOM_HALF_WIDTH_UM = 100.0

# The image drawn UNDER the cells in the zoom panels. H&E rather than the DAPI or
# morphology stains, because the question these slides answer is morphological — an
# oocyte is recognisable on H&E to anyone who reads ovary sections, and a call that
# disagrees with the histology is visibly wrong in a way no per-cell metric shows.
#
# Optional by nature: create_sdata only writes it when the sample was given an --he_image
# and its alignment matrix, so a cohort mixing aligned and unaligned samples is normal.
# Absent, the cells are drawn over white and the caption says so — falling back to a
# different stain would put two samples' panels on different backgrounds under one
# heading, which reads as a difference in the tissue.
ZOOM_BASE_IMAGE = "he_image"

# How opaque the cell fill sits over that image. Chosen by rendering the same window at
# 0.0, 0.35 and 0.6: at 0.0 the cluster is only a coloured rim and unreadable at a glance,
# at 0.6 the fills flatten the histology into blocks, and 0.35 keeps both — the stroma's
# fibre texture still runs under the cells while the cluster colour is plain.
ZOOM_FILL_ALPHA = 0.35

# Boundary line width, in points. The cells are drawn from the `cell_boundaries` SHAPES
# element rather than the `cell_labels` raster: at this magnification the vector polygon
# gives a clean edge where the raster's eroded contour gives a stepped one, and the width
# is a continuous point value instead of a whole number of pixels.
ZOOM_OUTLINE_WIDTH = 1.0

# The curated cell's own outline. Not black, which every other cell now carries — the
# target has to differ in kind, not merely in weight. White reads against both H&E's
# pink/purple and the turbo cluster fills, and unlike a saturated hue it cannot be
# mistaken for one more category in the palette.
ZOOM_TARGET_COLOR = "white"

# The target's outline weight, in the same points as ZOOM_OUTLINE_WIDTH. Heavier than its
# neighbours' so the eye lands on it first, but only slightly: the colour is what marks the
# cell, and at 3x the boundary was thick enough to eat into the cytoplasm it encircles and
# to hide how the segmentation actually traced the cell.
ZOOM_TARGET_OUTLINE_WIDTH = ZOOM_OUTLINE_WIDTH * 1.5

# The mark naming a zoom's window on the overview slide. Red is already this deck's "the one
# under discussion" mark, on the evidence heatmaps (see outline_calls) — the two never share
# a slide, and reusing it keeps one meaning for one colour rather than inventing a second
# mark for the same idea.
ZOOM_MARK_COLOR = "red"

# One colour per marker set for the transcript panel on the zoom slides, keyed by set name
# and applied in sorted-name order (spatialdata_plot takes a LIST ordered by the categories —
# a dict is silently ignored by this version). Deliberately NOT the cell type palette: these
# are the raw molecules a call was made from, not the call, and granulosa and theca are one
# joint cell type there while they are separate evidence here.
#
# Chosen against H&E rather than against each other: the background is pink and purple at
# middling luminance, so all three are high saturation and far off that hue. tab10's defaults
# were the first attempt and failed for theca — its green sat at roughly the stroma's own
# luminance, and at ~33 scattered molecules against granulosa's ~700 it was invisible.
#
# Applied by color_marker_points AFTER rendering, not by render_points' `palette` — that
# argument is silently ignored for points in this version (verified: the drawn colours stay
# tab10 whatever is passed), the same trap as `palette` on shapes.
MARKER_TX_COLORS = {"granulosa": "#00e5ff", "oocyte": "#ffd400", "theca": "#e60000"}

# Transcript dot size on the zoom panels, in the points units render_points takes on the
# matplotlib path (a window this size holds ~1,300 marker molecules, well under the 10k where
# spatialdata_plot switches to datashader). Big enough to read singly, small enough that a
# follicle's dense core stays granular rather than a solid blob.
MARKER_TX_POINT_SIZE = 2

# Forwarded to matplotlib-scalebar wherever a panel carries a scale. Its default draws the
# bar on an opaque white panel, which blanks the corner of the image underneath it — on a
# zoom that corner is tissue. Removing the box is most of the change; the rest is what the
# box was quietly doing, and each of these was picked by rendering the alternatives over a
# real zoom rather than by taste:
#   * `location` lower right, not the default upper right, where the bar collided with the
#     cells hanging past the top edge of the window and was clipped by the panel.
#   * `scale_loc` "top" with `sep` 1, so the label sits just above its bar. Without the box
#     the two defaulted to overlapping each other, which is what made the first attempt
#     unreadable.
#   * white, not black. Against fills at ZOOM_FILL_ALPHA over H&E a black bar disappears
#     entirely; white carries, and style_scalebar gives it a dark stroke so it survives the
#     pale corners too.
SCALEBAR_PARAMS = {"frameon": False, "location": "lower right", "scale_loc": "top",
                   "sep": 1, "border_pad": 0.6, "color": "white",
                   "font_properties": {"size": 7}}

# The switch for the above. OFF: boxed, the bar hid tissue; boxless, it stayed hard to read
# at any colour tried, because a 25 µm bar on a 200 µm window is short and thin against
# cells of exactly its own scale. The size information is not lost with it — every zoom is
# the same ZOOM_HALF_WIDTH_UM window and the caption says so in µm. Set True to bring it back;
# SCALEBAR_PARAMS and style_scalebar are kept rather than deleted for that reason.
SHOW_SCALEBAR = False

# The oocyte zoom section: the window map and the per-stage zooms. OFF, temporarily. It is
# the most expensive part of a render - a crop, an H&E read and a points materialization per
# stage per sample - and everything above it is read at section scale, so switching it off
# is how the rest of the deck is iterated on quickly. Set True to bring it back; nothing is
# deleted, and stage_representatives is simply not called while it is off.
SHOW_OOCYTE_ZOOMS = False

CURATED_OOCYTES = pd.DataFrame()
if OOCYTES_CSV.exists():
    CURATED_OOCYTES = pd.read_csv(OOCYTES_CSV)
    missing_cols = ({"cell_id", "Stage.Labels", "Quality", "cell_area"}
                    - set(CURATED_OOCYTES.columns))
    if missing_cols:
        raise ValueError(f"{OOCYTES_CSV} missing column(s): {sorted(missing_cols)}")
    CURATED_OOCYTES = CURATED_OOCYTES[
        ~CURATED_OOCYTES["Stage.Labels"].isin(OOCYTE_STAGE_EXCLUDE)]

# The per-cell QC columns each sample's panel shows, as (obs column, axis label, log).
#
# Every entry must already exist in obs — this deck derives no QC of its own, and a
# metric computed here would be a second definition of one create_sdata already emits.
#
# n_genes_by_transcripts, NOT n_genes_by_counts: the latter existed only because
# cluster_sdata* used to re-run calculate_qc_metrics with the default expr_type. That
# call is gone, so the column is gone with it, and create_sdata's own — computed once,
# before any filtering — is what clustered zarrs carry.
#
# pct_control is deliberately NOT here, despite being the Xenium-specific debris signal
# and now available from create_sdata. A violin is the wrong instrument for it: the
# metric is exactly 0 for most cells on a clean sample, so every cluster collapses to a
# spike at the baseline with a thin tail, and the one cluster that differs reads as a
# slightly fatter spike. The comparison it supports — which cluster is reading control
# probes — wants a per-cluster summary rather than a distribution.
QC_COLUMNS = [
    ("transcript_counts", "Transcripts", True),
    ("n_genes_by_transcripts", "Genes", True),
    ("cell_area", "Cell area (µm²)", True),
]

# sample -> overriding resolution, as the float the CSV records. Read once here so a
# malformed table fails the whole deck rather than every per-sample slide separately.
# Samples absent from it (or from a missing file) fall back to DEFAULT_RESOLUTION.
OVERRIDES = {}
if RESOLUTIONS_CSV.exists():
    chosen = pd.read_csv(RESOLUTIONS_CSV)
    missing_cols = {"sample", "resolution"} - set(chosen.columns)
    if missing_cols:
        raise ValueError(f"chosen_resolutions.csv missing column(s): {sorted(missing_cols)}")
    OVERRIDES = dict(zip(chosen["sample"].astype(str), chosen["resolution"].astype(float)))


# Every cell type this deck can assign: the follicle marker sets, which the reference
# does not contain, plus the reference's own major types. One vocabulary so a sample's
# calls live in one sheet and one tissue plot.
CELL_TYPE_VOCABULARY = sorted(MARKER_SETS) + list(REFERENCE.columns)

# The label for cells in no called cluster. Named rather than left as NaN so it takes a
# column in the composition tables — how much of a sample is unaccounted for is a result,
# not a gap, and on these samples it is most of the section.
UNASSIGNED = "unassigned"

# (sample, cell_type) -> list of cluster_v2 ids, from the hand-made sheet. A list because
# one cell type can span several clusters. An entry present but EMPTY means "judged not
# present in this sample", which is distinct from the pair being absent — absent means no
# judgement was made and the argmax stands.
CELL_TYPE_CALLS = {}
if CELL_TYPES_CSV.exists():
    called = pd.read_csv(CELL_TYPES_CSV, comment="#", dtype=str)
    missing_cols = {"sample", "cell_type", "cluster_v2"} - set(called.columns)
    if missing_cols:
        raise ValueError(
            f"{CELL_TYPES_CSV} missing column(s): {sorted(missing_cols)}")
    unknown = sorted(set(called["cell_type"]) - set(CELL_TYPE_VOCABULARY))
    if unknown:
        # A typo would otherwise become its own silent category that matches nothing, so
        # the call would vanish rather than fail.
        raise ValueError(
            f"{CELL_TYPES_CSV}: cell_type values {unknown} are not in the vocabulary "
            f"({CELL_TYPE_VOCABULARY})")
    for sample_id, cell_type, cluster in zip(called["sample"], called["cell_type"],
                                             called["cluster_v2"]):
        key = (str(sample_id), str(cell_type))
        CELL_TYPE_CALLS.setdefault(key, [])
        if not pd.isna(cluster) and str(cluster).strip():
            CELL_TYPE_CALLS[key].append(str(cluster).strip())


# Cluster-id colours here encode ORDER, not identity: the v2 ids are 1..n in
# dendrogram order, so adjacent ids are transcriptionally adjacent. Sampling a multi-hue
# ordered colormap ALONG that order makes proximity read as colour similarity — the
# opposite of a categorical palette like tab20, which maximises adjacent contrast and so
# hides the very ordering the relabel created. The numeric id is always drawn on the UMAP
# (legend on data), so colour is never the sole identity channel.
#
# Matches sammy_r21's sample_summary deck (see oir-analysis HANDOFF.md, "Palette"). turbo,
# trimmed off both ends because its extremes are near-black and near-maroon; kept off the
# correlation heatmap's viridis to avoid a same-colour collision.
CLUSTER_CMAP = "turbo"
CLUSTER_CMAP_RANGE = (0.05, 0.95)


def _srgb_to_lab(rgb):
    """sRGB triples in [0, 1] -> CIE Lab (D65).

    Only used to space the cluster palette; nothing else in the deck needs Lab.
    """
    rgb = np.asarray(rgb, dtype=float)
    lin = np.where(rgb <= 0.04045, rgb / 12.92, ((rgb + 0.055) / 1.055) ** 2.4)
    xyz = lin @ np.array([[0.4124564, 0.3575761, 0.1804375],
                          [0.2126729, 0.7151522, 0.0721750],
                          [0.0193339, 0.1191920, 0.9503041]]).T
    t = xyz / np.array([0.95047, 1.0, 1.08883])
    d = 6 / 29
    f = np.where(t > d ** 3, np.cbrt(t), t / (3 * d ** 2) + 4 / 29)
    return np.stack([116 * f[..., 1] - 16,
                     500 * (f[..., 0] - f[..., 1]),
                     200 * (f[..., 1] - f[..., 2])], axis=-1)


def gradient_colors(n, cmap_name=CLUSTER_CMAP, span=CLUSTER_CMAP_RANGE):
    """n ordered hex colours, spaced at equal PERCEPTUAL distance along the colormap.

    Sampling a colormap at equal steps of its own parameter leaves some neighbours far
    closer than others — across turbo the greens crowd together while the blues spread.
    Walking the colormap at constant CIE Lab arc length instead evens those gaps out, which
    matters here because adjacent ids are transcriptionally adjacent and so are the ones a
    reader compares.
    """
    lo, hi = span
    cmap = plt.get_cmap(cmap_name)
    # Dense walk of the ramp, then invert its cumulative arc length: interpolating n equally
    # spaced arc lengths back to colormap positions gives the perceptually even sample points.
    ts = np.linspace(lo, hi, 2000)
    lab = _srgb_to_lab([cmap(t)[:3] for t in ts])
    cumulative = np.concatenate([[0], np.cumsum(np.linalg.norm(np.diff(lab, axis=0), axis=1))])
    return [to_hex(cmap(t)) for t in np.interp(np.linspace(0, cumulative[-1], n), cumulative, ts)]


def style_on_data_labels(ax, color="white", outline="black", linewidth=1.5):
    """Restyle scanpy's on-data cluster labels to `color` text with an `outline` stroke.

    scanpy's legend_fontoutline hardcodes a white stroke around black text, which is hard to
    read on light clusters — and turbo's middle is pale yellow-green. Flip it to white text
    with a black outline, which reads on both ends of the ramp. The cluster labels are the
    only Text artists scanpy adds to the axes body, so restyling ax.texts hits exactly them.

    The stroke has to stay THIN relative to the glyph. withStroke widens the outline
    outward and inward from the path, so a heavy one on a small digit closes over the
    counters and the label reads as a dark blob with a suggestion of a number inside it —
    which is what 2.5 pt under a 7 pt font did here. Raise the font before the stroke.
    """
    for t in ax.texts:
        t.set_color(color)
        t.set_path_effects([patheffects.withStroke(linewidth=linewidth, foreground=outline)])


def umap_figure_height(coords, panel_width, chrome_in):
    """Figure height, in inches, for a UMAP slide fitted to the embedding not to the slide.

    match_umap_axes puts every UMAP on equal aspect, which shrinks the axes BOX to the
    embedding's shape and then centres that box in whatever space the figure gave it. A
    height taken from the slide rather than from the data is therefore not spent on a bigger
    UMAP — it becomes a band of empty slide above and below the panel, which is what every
    one of these slides looked like. Sizing the figure to the embedding spends it on the
    panel instead.

    `panel_width` is the inches the AXES itself can use: subtract a legend that sits outside
    it before calling. `chrome_in` is everything vertical the panel does not occupy — the
    suptitle, any panel titles, a colourbar — and is fitted against the rendered slide
    rather than derived, since tight_layout distributes whatever is left over. It only has
    to be close enough not to squeeze the panel or leave a second band.

    Capped at the slide's height budget so a TALL embedding letterboxes sideways as it
    always has, rather than growing a figure that no longer fits the layout.
    """
    span_x = (coords[:, 0].max() - coords[:, 0].min()) * (1 + 2 * UMAP_MARGIN)
    span_y = (coords[:, 1].max() - coords[:, 1].min()) * (1 + 2 * UMAP_MARGIN)
    return min(FIGSIZE[1] * 0.95, panel_width * span_y / span_x + chrome_in)


def match_umap_axes(ax, coords):
    """Put a UMAP panel on equal aspect and the sample's full extent.

    Every UMAP in a sample's section shows the same embedding, so they should differ only
    in scale — but matplotlib stretches data to fill whatever box it is given, and the
    boxes are not the same shape: the cluster UMAP has one axes across most of the slide
    while the marker panel has three side by side. Left alone the same embedding comes out
    tall and narrow on one slide and wide on another, and a reader comparing an island's
    position between them is comparing two different distortions.

    Equal aspect fixes the shape and the shared limits fix the framing, so the panels are
    the same picture at different sizes. The cost is letterboxing — a wide box around a
    tall embedding leaves margin at the sides — which is the right trade: whitespace is
    honest where a stretched embedding is not. UMAP axes carry no units and are not drawn,
    so nothing else needs to change.
    """
    x, y = coords[:, 0], coords[:, 1]
    pad_x = (x.max() - x.min()) * UMAP_MARGIN
    pad_y = (y.max() - y.min()) * UMAP_MARGIN
    ax.set_xlim(x.min() - pad_x, x.max() + pad_x)
    ax.set_ylim(y.min() - pad_y, y.max() + pad_y)
    ax.set_aspect("equal")


def md_table(df):
    """Render a DataFrame as a markdown table.

    Built by hand rather than via df.style, which is HTML-only and renders as nothing in
    pptx, or df.to_markdown, which needs tabulate — not in the pipeline container.

    Wrapped in blank lines so the pipes start their own block. Without them Pandoc reads
    them as a lazy continuation of the caption paragraph above and prints them verbatim
    instead of building a table.
    """
    header = "| " + " | ".join(str(c) for c in df.columns) + " |"
    rule = "| " + " | ".join("---" for _ in df.columns) + " |"
    rows = ["| " + " | ".join(str(v) for v in row) + " |"
            for row in df.itertuples(index=False)]
    display(Markdown("\n".join(["", ""] + [header, rule] + rows + ["", ""])))


def add_cluster_ids(adata, key, levels, name):
    """Write a renumbered 1..n categorical for `levels` into obs, plus its palette.

    `levels` is the original leiden labels in the order the numbering assigns, so
    position i becomes cluster i + 1. Renumbering into obs once — rather than telling
    every plot function about the ordering — is what lets scanpy draw the UMAP and the
    violins straight from the object: both read the same column, so they cannot end up on
    different numberings by accident. The categories are set explicitly so 10 sorts after
    9 rather than lexically, and so an empty cluster still holds its slot.

    The palette goes into uns under scanpy's own `<key>_colors` convention, which
    sc.pl.* picks up without being passed a palette at all.
    """
    ids = [str(i + 1) for i in range(len(levels))]
    mapping = {level: str(i + 1) for i, level in enumerate(levels)}
    adata.obs[name] = pd.Categorical(adata.obs[key].map(mapping), categories=ids)
    adata.uns[f"{name}_colors"] = gradient_colors(len(levels))


def centroid_correlation(sample, corr, order):
    """One slide's figure: the same correlation matrix under both numberings, side by side.

    Rows and columns are ordered by hierarchical clustering, symmetrically, so the matrix
    stays symmetric and transcriptionally similar clusters sit adjacent as blocks. Only the
    TICKS differ between the two panels — the matrix is identical, drawn in dendrogram
    order both times.

    Left is keyed by the v1 ids, which therefore read out of numeric sequence;
    right by the v2 ids, which read 1..n because that numbering IS this ordering.
    Side by side rather than on consecutive slides so the rename is visible in place — a
    reader sees which v1 cluster each v2 id renames without chasing a mapping
    line in the caption.

    The diagonal is kept rather than blanked. It is 1 by construction, but on this data the
    off-diagonal already reaches ~0.99, so including it moves vmax by about a point and
    costs nothing.

    The drawing is a loop over the two panels rather than a general heatmap helper: both
    panels take the same square symmetric matrix and differ only in their tick labels, so a
    helper's row/col-label and x/y-label pairs would carry no information here. (sammy_r21
    keeps such a helper because it also draws non-square cross-sample matrices; this deck
    has only the self-self case.)
    """
    values = corr[np.ix_(order, order)]
    # Derived once, so both panels and the shared colorbar are on the same ramp by
    # construction rather than by each panel happening to compute it from the same matrix.
    vmin, vmax = float(values.min()), float(values.max())

    # order[p] is a 0-based v1 rank position; +1 makes it the printed v1 id.
    panels = (
        ([int(p) + 1 for p in order], "Cluster", "numbered by size"),
        (list(range(1, len(order) + 1)), "Cluster", "numbered by similarity"),
    )

    fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(12.5, 5.2), constrained_layout=True)
    for ax, (ids, axis_label, title) in zip(axes, panels):
        im = ax.imshow(values, cmap="viridis", aspect="auto", vmin=vmin, vmax=vmax)
        for i in range(len(ids)):
            for j in range(len(ids)):
                # Threshold on the colour, not the value: mid-viridis is light enough that
                # black reads better. The leading zero is dropped to keep labels narrow.
                light = (values[i, j] - vmin) / (vmax - vmin) > 0.5 if vmax > vmin else True
                ax.text(j, i, f"{values[i, j]:.2f}".replace("0.", "."),
                        ha="center", va="center", fontsize=7,
                        color="black" if light else "white")
        ax.set_xticks(range(len(ids)), [str(c) for c in ids], fontsize=8)
        ax.set_yticks(range(len(ids)), [str(c) for c in ids], fontsize=8)
        ax.set_xlabel(axis_label, fontsize=9)
        ax.set_ylabel(axis_label, fontsize=9)
        ax.set_title(title, fontsize=8)

    # One shared colorbar — both panels are the same matrix on the same scale.
    cbar = fig.colorbar(im, ax=list(axes), fraction=0.046, pad=0.02)
    cbar.ax.set_ylabel("Spearman r", fontsize=8)
    cbar.ax.tick_params(labelsize=7)

    fig.suptitle(f"{sample} · {len(order)} clusters", fontsize=9)
    plt.show()
    plt.close(fig)


def reference_correlation(sample, corr, resolved, n_genes):
    """One slide's figure: each cluster's centroid against the major cell types.

    Spearman, over every gene the sample shares with the reference. See the note where
    REFERENCE is loaded for what that costs in margin.

    The call is NOT thresholded, and no cell type is written into obs here. What the
    slide reports is the best match, its correlation, and its MARGIN over the runner-up;
    reading those is the judgement, and it belongs to whoever reads the deck. A cluster
    can top a column simply because the reference has nowhere better to put it: this
    reference holds four stromal-compartment types and no follicle or epithelium, so an
    oocyte or granulosa cluster is assigned to whichever of the four it least badly
    resembles. Those clusters are identifiable on the marker-score slide instead, which
    is why it sits immediately before this one.

    A low r with a small margin is the honest reading of "this cluster is not in the
    reference" — treat it that way rather than accepting the argmax.
    """
    evidence_heatmap(
        sample, corr, resolved,
        f"{sample} · cluster centroids vs major cell types · {n_genes:,} shared genes",
        raw_label="Spearman r", column_label="within each cell type",
        row_label="within each cluster")


def marker_dotplot(adata, sample, name):
    """One slide's figure: the marker genes themselves, per cluster.

    The scored heatmap says which cluster owns a set; this says WHY, and the two are
    worth having side by side. A set score cannot distinguish a cluster expressing every
    marker from one expressing two of them strongly, and on sets this small — 5 to 10
    genes at MARKER_MAX_SCORE = 1 — that difference decides whether a call is real.

    Dot area is the fraction of the cluster's cells with any count for the gene, and
    colour is mean expression among all of them. The fraction is the more robust of the
    two on Xenium: at ~200 transcripts per cell against a 5K panel, a genuine oocyte
    often has zero counts for a given marker, so mean expression is noisy where "half the
    cluster expresses it at all" is not.

    Read from layers["lognorm"] rather than X, which cluster_sdata leaves scaled — a
    dotplot of z-like values would colour by how unusual a gene is for a cell, not by
    how much of it there is. standard_scale="var" then puts each gene on its own 0-1
    range down the column, so a quiet marker is visible beside an abundant one.
    """
    if "lognorm" not in adata.layers:
        raise KeyError(
            f"{sample}: layers['lognorm'] is missing. cluster_sdata writes it alongside "
            "counts; re-run it over this sample rather than reading the scaled X."
        )
    present = {set_name: [g for g in genes if g in adata.var_names]
               for set_name, genes in MARKER_SETS.items()}
    present = {k: v for k, v in present.items() if v}
    if not present:
        raise ValueError(f"{sample}: no marker genes from any set are on this panel.")

    # No figure title. dotplot lays out its own axes and puts the gene-group brackets
    # directly above the main panel, and BOTH a suptitle and scanpy's own `title` land on
    # top of them — tried in that order. The slide heading and caption carry the sample
    # and the score threshold instead, which is where this deck puts context anyway.
    axes = sc.pl.dotplot(
        adata,
        var_names=present,          # dict -> genes grouped and bracketed by set
        groupby=name,
        layer="lognorm",
        standard_scale="var",
        cmap="viridis",
        figsize=(FIGSIZE[0] * 0.92, FIGSIZE[1] * 0.82),
        show=False,
    )
    fig = axes["mainplot_ax"].get_figure() if isinstance(axes, dict) else plt.gcf()
    plt.show()
    plt.close(fig)


def marker_set_scores(centroids):
    """Cluster x marker-set scores: the mean of the set's markers in each centroid.

    Deliberately just a mean. Standardizing each gene across clusters before averaging
    was tried and dropped: on both test ROIs it picked the same cluster for granulosa and
    for oocyte as the plain mean did, and differed only on theca, where the dotplot shows
    no signal at all — so it changed the answer only where there was no answer. A step
    that cannot be shown to change a conclusion should not be in the middle of one.

    Built from centroids, not per cell. sc.tl.score_genes on this data scores a 7-gene
    set against ~200 transcripts drawn from 5,101 genes, so most cells hold zero of the
    set even in the cluster that owns it, and the per-cell score is mostly sampling
    noise; averaging within a cluster afterwards is the same aggregation by a worse path.
    It also sidesteps score_genes' control set, which is capped at the size of the gene
    list — a 5-gene theca set would be judged against a 5-gene background.

    The values are therefore log1p CP10K expression, in the same units as the centroids,
    and are NOT comparable between sets: granulosa markers sit near 0.75 in every cluster
    of these samples while oocyte markers sit near 0.06, so the same number means very
    different things in two columns. The heatmap colours each column on its own range for
    exactly this reason.

    A gene absent from the panel is dropped, and a set with none left scores NaN rather
    than 0: no evidence is not evidence of absence.
    """
    scores = {}
    for set_name, genes in MARKER_SETS.items():
        present = [g for g in genes if g in centroids.columns]
        scores[set_name] = (centroids[present].mean(axis=1) if present
                            else pd.Series(np.nan, index=centroids.index))
    return pd.DataFrame(scores)


def evidence_heatmap(sample, values, resolved, suptitle, raw_label,
                     column_label, row_label):
    """One slide's figure: a clusters x cell-type matrix under three normalizations.

    The same matrix three times, because the three answer different questions and no one
    of them answers all three:

      raw       absolute magnitude, in whatever units the matrix is in.
      column    down a column, which cluster is highest for that cell type. The column's
                own baseline drops out.
      row       across a row, which cell type is highest in that cluster. This is the one
                that points at an annotation.

    Each panel PRINTS the values it colours by, so a number always matches its own shade.
    Reading across panels is then reading three different quantities, which is the point.

    Shared by both evidence families — the marker means and the reference correlations —
    so the two slides are the same figure over a different matrix rather than two
    implementations that agree today. Their units differ, which is what the label
    arguments carry.
    """
    raw = values.to_numpy(dtype=float)

    def normalize(matrix, axis):
        lo = np.nanmin(matrix, axis=axis, keepdims=True)
        span = np.nanmax(matrix, axis=axis, keepdims=True) - lo
        return (matrix - lo) / np.where(span > 0, span, np.nan)

    panels = [
        (raw, "raw", raw_label),
        (normalize(raw, 0), "column-normalized", column_label),
        (normalize(raw, 1), "row-normalized", row_label),
    ]

    fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(FIGSIZE[0], FIGSIZE[1]), constrained_layout=True)
    for ax, (matrix, title, bar_label) in zip(axes, panels):
        finite = matrix[np.isfinite(matrix)]
        vmin, vmax = (float(finite.min()), float(finite.max())) if finite.size else (0.0, 1.0)
        image = ax.imshow(matrix, cmap="viridis", aspect="auto", vmin=vmin, vmax=vmax)
        ax.set_xticks(range(values.shape[1]))
        ax.set_xticklabels(values.columns, rotation=45, ha="right", fontsize=7)
        ax.set_yticks(range(values.shape[0]))
        ax.set_yticklabels(values.index, fontsize=7)
        ax.set_title(title, fontsize=8)
        for row in range(matrix.shape[0]):
            for col in range(matrix.shape[1]):
                value = matrix[row, col]
                if not np.isfinite(value):
                    continue
                # Text colour off this panel's own scale, so it stays legible under
                # whichever normalization is driving the shade.
                shade = (value - vmin) / (vmax - vmin) if vmax > vmin else 0.0
                ax.text(col, row, f"{value:.2f}", ha="center", va="center", fontsize=6,
                        color="black" if shade > 0.55 else "white")
        # The same boxes on all three panels. The call is one decision made on the raw
        # values; drawing it only on the raw panel would suggest the normalizations each
        # produce their own, when the normalized panels are the same numbers rescaled.
        outline_calls(ax, values.index, values.columns, resolved)
        bar = fig.colorbar(image, ax=ax, fraction=0.045)
        bar.set_label(bar_label, fontsize=6)
        bar.ax.tick_params(labelsize=5)

    axes[0].set_ylabel("cluster", fontsize=8)
    fig.suptitle(suptitle, fontsize=9, x=0.01, ha="left")
    plt.show()
    plt.close(fig)


def marker_score_heatmap(sample, scores, resolved):
    """One slide's figure: the cluster x marker-set means under three normalizations.

    The same matrix three times, because the three answer different questions and no one
    of them answers all three:

      raw       absolute magnitude. Granulosa markers really are more abundant than
                oocyte markers here — near 0.75 against near 0.06 in every cluster —
                and that is worth seeing rather than normalizing away.
      column    within a set, which cluster is highest: "which cluster is the granulosa
                one". The set's own baseline drops out.
      row       within a cluster, which set is highest: "what is this cluster most
                like". This is the one that points at an annotation.

    Each panel PRINTS the values it colours by, so a number always matches its own
    shade. Reading across panels is then reading three different quantities, which is
    the point — the raw panel keeps the magnitudes the normalized ones discard.

    Beware the normalized panels where a set has no signal. Scaled to its own range,
    theca's 0.11-0.53 spread paints its best cluster as brightly as granulosa's genuine
    2.13, and nothing in the colour says which is which. That is what the raw panel is
    for, and why nothing here is boxed.

    KNOWN LIMITATION of the row panel, left as-is deliberately. Because the sets sit at
    very different levels, the row maximum is granulosa in almost every cluster on these
    samples — six of seven on ROI1_A — purely because granulosa markers are ~10x more
    abundant than oocyte markers, not because those clusters are granulosa. Cluster 3
    reads 1.00 there on a raw value of 0.88, beside cluster 7's genuine 2.13. Read the
    row panel only against the raw one. Making it mean what it looks like it means would
    require standardizing each set across clusters BEFORE normalizing along the row, so
    the sets are commensurate first — the same z-score dropped from the column question,
    where it changed no argmax, but which the row question actually needs.
    """
    evidence_heatmap(
        sample, scores, resolved,
        f"{sample} · mean marker expression per cluster",
        raw_label="log1p CP10K", column_label="within each set",
        row_label="within each cluster")



def marker_umaps(adata, sample):
    """One slide's figure: each marker set's mean expression on the UMAP.

    The heatmap says WHICH cluster owns a set; this says whether the signal is tight.
    A set concentrated in one region is a cell type; one smeared thinly across the
    embedding is a set of genes that happen to be broadly expressed, and both give the
    same cluster mean.

    The value is the plain mean of the set's markers in each cell, from the same
    log-normalized layer the dotplot reads and the same mean the cluster heatmap takes —
    the cluster values are these aggregated, so the two slides cannot tell different
    stories. Not sc.tl.score_genes: its background correction is what made the earlier
    version of this slide hard to read, and its control set is capped at the size of the
    gene list, which for a 5-gene set is no background at all.

    Expect most cells to read zero. At ~200 transcripts against a 5,101-gene panel a
    genuine oocyte often carries none of the 7 oocyte markers, so the panel is mostly
    dark with a bright island. That is the honest picture of the evidence rather than a
    fault in the plot, and it is why the cluster-level heatmap is the slide that carries
    the call.
    """
    if "lognorm" not in adata.layers:
        raise KeyError(
            f"{sample}: layers['lognorm'] is missing. cluster_sdata writes it alongside "
            "counts; re-run it over this sample rather than reading the scaled X."
        )
    present = {name: [g for g in genes if g in adata.var_names]
               for name, genes in MARKER_SETS.items()}
    present = {k: v for k, v in present.items() if v}

    columns = []
    for set_name, genes in present.items():
        column = f"mean_{set_name}"
        block = adata[:, genes].layers["lognorm"]
        # .A1 on a sparse row-mean gives a flat array; np.asarray covers the dense case.
        mean = block.mean(axis=1)
        adata.obs[column] = np.asarray(mean).ravel()
        columns.append((column, f"{set_name} ({len(genes)} genes)"))

    # Three panels across a fixed width fixes the panel width; the embedding's own aspect
    # then fixes the height they can use. Chrome here is the suptitle, each panel's title
    # and the horizontal colourbar with its tick labels — the most of any UMAP slide.
    height = umap_figure_height(adata.obsm["X_umap"], FIGSIZE[0] / len(columns), 1.1)
    fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, len(columns), figsize=(FIGSIZE[0], height), squeeze=False)
    for ax, (column, title) in zip(axes.ravel(), columns):
        # Cells sorted low-to-high so the expressing ones are drawn last: at this
        # sparsity the bright cells are a small minority and would otherwise be buried
        # under the zeros they sit among.
        order = np.argsort(adata.obs[column].to_numpy(), kind="stable")
        sc.pl.embedding(
            adata[order],
            basis="umap",
            color=column,
            cmap="magma",
            frameon=False,
            title=title,
            # Scanpy's own colourbar is a full-height bar to the right of each panel. With
            # three panels on one slide that is three tall bars taking width from the
            # embeddings and setting the row's height, which is what left the UMAPs small
            # in a field of white. Suppressed here and re-drawn horizontally below.
            colorbar_loc=None,
            ax=ax,
            show=False,
        )
        match_umap_axes(ax, adata.obsm["X_umap"])
        ax.title.set_fontsize(8)

        # Horizontal bar under the panel, off the PathCollection scanpy left on the axes —
        # the same handle qc_report reaches for when it needs to touch a scanpy scatter
        # after the fact. Underneath rather than beside because these panels are wider
        # than they are tall once the aspect is fixed, so horizontal space is the scarce
        # one; and each set keeps its own scale, since the sets are not comparable.
        # Kept small deliberately: the panel is read for WHERE the signal sits, and the bar
        # is only there to say what the ramp means, so it should not compete with the
        # embedding for either height or width.
        bar = fig.colorbar(ax.collections[-1], ax=ax, orientation="horizontal",
                           fraction=0.03, pad=0.02, shrink=0.55)
        bar.ax.tick_params(labelsize=6)
        bar.outline.set_visible(False)

    fig.suptitle(f"{sample} · mean marker expression per cell",
                 fontsize=9, x=0.01, ha="left")
    fig.tight_layout()
    plt.show()
    plt.close(fig)



def umap_clusters(adata, sample, name):
    """One slide's figure: this sample's UMAP, coloured by one of the two numberings.

    Drawn by sc.pl.umap from the object itself: the numbering lives in obs[name] and its
    palette in uns, so both versions of this slide are the same call with a different
    column — they cannot drift apart in styling.

    The ids are carried BOTH ways: on the data at each cluster's median, and in a legend
    beside the panel. They answer different questions. The on-data label says which lobe is
    which without a colour lookup, which is the whole point of the slide; the legend says
    which id owns a colour even where labels collide, and they will collide — a test crop's
    7 clusters place cleanly, but the real whole-slide samples run to 16-28 and several
    share a lobe. Either alone leaves a gap the other covers, and the legend is what the
    tissue slides already carry, so the two views of one numbering agree.

    Cells are handed over sorted by descending cluster size, so the small clusters are
    drawn last and land on top. scanpy draws one scatter in row order, and the reverse
    buries a 300-cell cluster under a 16,000-cell one wherever they overlap. The sort is a
    view, so no count matrix is copied to do it.

    Marker size is left to scanpy, which already scales it as 120000 / n_cells.
    """
    # Room for the legend beside the panel, the same reservation the tissue slides and the
    # cell type UMAP make, so the panels line up in width across the section.
    width = FIGSIZE[0] * 0.62
    fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(width, umap_figure_height(
        adata.obsm["X_umap"], width - SPATIAL_LEGEND_WIDTH, 0.25)))

    sizes = adata.obs[name].value_counts()
    order = np.argsort(-adata.obs[name].map(sizes).to_numpy(), kind="stable")

    sc.pl.umap(
        adata[order],
        color=name,
        # On-data labels are scanpy's; the margin legend is not, and is rebuilt below —
        # scanpy's own takes the panel's width rather than the space reserved for it, and
        # orders its keys by draw order.
        legend_loc="on data",
        # 10, not the 7 the margin text uses: this label has to be picked out against 20,000
        # dots rather than read off a quiet margin, and the size is what lets
        # style_on_data_labels' outline stay thin enough to keep the digit open.
        legend_fontsize=10,
        legend_fontweight="bold",
        # UMAP axes carry no interpretable units — drop the frame entirely.
        frameon=False,
        title="",
        colorbar_loc=None,
        ax=ax,
        show=False,
    )
    style_on_data_labels(ax)
    match_umap_axes(ax, adata.obsm["X_umap"])

    # Proxy handles from the same uns palette the scatter was drawn from, keyed in NUMERIC
    # order — the draw order above is by cluster size, so handles taken off the axes would
    # read 2, 1, 5, 3... The tissue slide reorders its own handles for exactly this reason.
    # Two columns past 12 ids, where one column runs taller than the panel it labels.
    levels = list(adata.obs[name].cat.categories)
    colors = adata.uns[f"{name}_colors"]
    handles = [plt.Line2D([], [], marker="o", linestyle="none", markersize=4,
                          color=colors[int(level) - 1]) for level in levels]
    ax.legend(handles, [str(level) for level in levels],
              loc="center left", bbox_to_anchor=(1.0, 0.5), frameon=False,
              fontsize=7, handletextpad=0.2, title=name, title_fontsize=7,
              ncol=1 if len(levels) <= 12 else 2, columnspacing=0.8)

    n_clusters = adata.obs[name].nunique()
    fig.suptitle(f"{sample} · {adata.n_obs:,} cells · {n_clusters} clusters",
                 fontsize=9, x=0.01, ha="left")
    fig.tight_layout()
    plt.show()
    plt.close(fig)


def resolve_cell_types(sample, evidence, valid_clusters):
    """Which clusters answer for each cell type, as (cell_type -> list of v2 ids).

    `evidence` is one frame of clusters x cell types — the marker means and the reference
    correlations concatenated — so both families are assigned by one rule.

    The default is the argmax down each COLUMN: the cluster scoring highest for that cell
    type. Per column and not per row, for both families and for the same reason. Marker
    means are not comparable between sets, so a row maximum is baseline rather than
    biology. Reference correlations ARE on one scale but are not equally achievable: in
    stroma-dominated tissue every centroid resembles the Stromal profile, so a row
    maximum is Stromal almost everywhere — on ROI1_B it called Stromal at 0.54 over
    Immune at 0.51 for the one cluster whose Immune correlation was five to ten times
    every other cluster's. Down the column that cluster is unmistakable.

    The cost of column argmax is that it names at most one cluster per cell type, so a
    section splitting into several stromal clusters gets one of them coloured. That is
    what the sheet is for: add rows.

    Where two types' argmax is the same cluster, the conflict is resolved rather than
    shared — see the greedy pass below.

    A hand-made entry replaces the default for that (sample, cell_type) entirely. An
    entry present but empty means "not in this sample" and returns nothing, which is how
    a judgement overrides the default DOWNWARD — the argmax always exists, even for a
    cell type with no signal, so without this theca could never be dismissed.
    """
    resolved = {}
    hand_called = set()
    for cell_type in evidence.columns:
        if (sample, cell_type) in CELL_TYPE_CALLS:
            called = CELL_TYPE_CALLS[(sample, cell_type)]
            unknown = [c for c in called if c not in valid_clusters]
            if unknown:
                # Warn rather than raise: a stale sheet should not take a cohort's render
                # down, but a silently dropped call would be worse than a noisy one.
                print(f"WARNING {sample}/{cell_type}: cluster(s) {unknown} not in this "
                      f"sample (has {sorted(valid_clusters, key=int)}) — ignored. The "
                      f"numbering moves when the clustering changes; re-derive the calls.")
            resolved[cell_type] = [c for c in called if c in valid_clusters]
            hand_called.update(resolved[cell_type])

    # One cluster answers for at most one cell type, so the argmaxes have to be resolved
    # against each other rather than taken independently. Two types whose argmax is the
    # same cluster used to share it and be labelled with both names joined; a joined label
    # cannot be a composition column, and counting the cluster under both types would
    # double count its cells.
    #
    # Resolved greedily by STRENGTH OF CLAIM: each type's lead over its own runner-up,
    # measured on the column's own 0-1 scale so a marker mean and a correlation are
    # comparable. The strongest claim is settled first and takes its cluster; a type whose
    # best cluster is already taken falls through to its next best. Every type therefore
    # still gets a cluster, and the type that wanted one most gets the one it wanted.
    #
    # Hand calls are not part of this. They are placed first, above, and the clusters they
    # name are removed from what the argmaxes can take — a judgement in the sheet outranks
    # any lead computed here.
    def claim_strength(cell_type):
        column = evidence[cell_type].dropna()
        if column.empty:
            return -np.inf
        span = column.max() - column.min()
        if span <= 0:
            return 0.0
        scaled = ((column - column.min()) / span).sort_values(ascending=False)
        return float(scaled.iloc[0] - scaled.iloc[1]) if len(scaled) > 1 else 1.0

    taken = set(hand_called)
    for cell_type in sorted((c for c in evidence.columns if c not in resolved),
                            key=claim_strength, reverse=True):
        column = evidence[cell_type].dropna().sort_values(ascending=False)
        free = [str(cluster) for cluster in column.index if str(cluster) not in taken]
        resolved[cell_type] = free[:1]
        taken.update(resolved[cell_type])
    return {cell_type: resolved[cell_type] for cell_type in evidence.columns}


def cell_type_labels(resolved):
    """v2 cluster id -> label, one cell type per cluster.

    Clusters used to carry every type that claimed them, joined with " + ". They no
    longer can: resolve_cell_types settles conflicts so a cluster answers for one type,
    which is what lets the composition tables have a column per type and count each cell
    once. The join is kept in the formatting below only so a hand-made sheet naming one
    cluster under two types still renders rather than dropping one silently.
    """
    by_cluster = {}
    for cell_type, clusters in resolved.items():
        for cluster in clusters:
            by_cluster.setdefault(cluster, []).append(cell_type)
    return {cluster: " + ".join(sorted(types)) for cluster, types in by_cluster.items()}


def outline_calls(ax, row_labels, col_labels, resolved):
    """Box the cluster each cell type was assigned to, on an evidence heatmap.

    The heatmaps show the evidence; the assignment is an argmax read off it. Drawing the
    box makes the two one object — without it a reader has to run the argmax by eye down
    every column and hope they agree with what the tissue plots were coloured by.

    One style regardless of where the call came from. A hand-made call in
    cell_type_annotations.csv REPLACES the default rather than sitting beside it, so the
    box means the same thing either way: this is the cluster answering for that cell type.
    Marking the source here would answer a question about the sheet rather than about the
    evidence, and the emitted cluster_annotations.csv already records it per row in its
    `source` column.

    A hand call naming several clusters boxes all of them, and one naming none — the
    "not present in this sample" judgement — boxes nothing, which is the honest picture of
    a cell type that was considered and dismissed.
    """
    positions = {str(label): i for i, label in enumerate(row_labels)}
    for col, cell_type in enumerate(col_labels):
        for cluster in resolved.get(cell_type, []):
            row = positions.get(str(cluster))
            if row is None:
                continue
            ax.add_patch(Rectangle((col - 0.5, row - 0.5), 1, 1, fill=False,
                                   edgecolor="red", linewidth=1.6, zorder=4))


def cell_type_palette(labels):
    """Cell type label -> colour, in the sorted order every cell type slide draws them.

    Shared by the three slides that colour by cell type — the UMAP, the tissue plot and
    the oocyte zoom — so a label is the same colour on all of them. They are read against
    each other, and the palette depends on how many labels a sample resolved, so three
    copies of `gradient_colors(len(...))` would agree only as long as each was handed the
    same dict.
    """
    ordered = sorted(set(labels.values()))
    return dict(zip(ordered, gradient_colors(max(len(ordered), 1))))


def annotated_umap(adata, sample, name, labels, title):
    """One slide's figure: the UMAP coloured by cell type rather than cluster id.

    Mirrors the tissue plot of the same calls — same palette, same grey for unassigned,
    same title — so the pair reads as one statement seen two ways. The tissue plot says
    where a called cell type sits in the section; this says whether it is coherent in
    expression space. A call covering a compact island is a different claim from one
    spread over half a lobe, and the tissue plot cannot distinguish them.
    """
    coords = adata.obsm["X_umap"]
    # The legend sits outside the axes, so tight_layout takes its width off the panel — the
    # height has to be fitted to what the panel actually gets, not to the whole figure.
    # SPATIAL_LEGEND_WIDTH is the same reservation spatial_cell_types makes for the same
    # legend on the tissue slide this one is read beside.
    width = FIGSIZE[0] * 0.62
    fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(width, umap_figure_height(
        coords, width - SPATIAL_LEGEND_WIDTH, 0.25)))

    called = adata.obs[name].astype(str).map(labels)
    unassigned = called.isna().to_numpy()
    ax.scatter(coords[unassigned, 0], coords[unassigned, 1], color="0.85",
               label="unassigned", s=2, alpha=1.0, edgecolors="none", rasterized=True)

    for label, color in cell_type_palette(labels).items():
        m = (called == label).to_numpy()
        if m.any():
            ax.scatter(coords[m, 0], coords[m, 1], color=color, label=label,
                       s=2, alpha=1.0, edgecolors="none", rasterized=True)

    match_umap_axes(ax, coords)
    ax.set_xticks([]); ax.set_yticks([])
    for spine in ax.spines.values():
        spine.set_visible(False)
    ax.legend(loc="center left", bbox_to_anchor=(1.0, 0.5), frameon=False,
              fontsize=7, markerscale=6, handletextpad=0.2, title="cell type",
              title_fontsize=7)
    n_called = int((~unassigned).sum())
    fig.suptitle(f"{sample} · {title} · {n_called:,} of {adata.n_obs:,} cells assigned",
                 fontsize=9, x=0.01, ha="left")
    fig.tight_layout()
    plt.show()
    plt.close(fig)


def tissue_figure(adata, legend_width=SPATIAL_LEGEND_WIDTH):
    """Figure, axes and marker size for a slide drawn in tissue coordinates.

    Three things are specific to tissue coordinates and all three would be wrong on
    defaults. The FIGURE is shaped to the tissue's own aspect, because equal aspect is
    non-negotiable here and a fixed box would render a wide strip as a band across an empty
    slide. The MARKER is sized from the axes area and the cell count, since one constant
    cannot serve a 21k-cell strip and a 700k-cell section. And y is INVERTED — that part is
    style_tissue_axes, since it has to happen after the data is drawn.

    get_position() is the pre-tight_layout fraction of the figure, close enough to size a
    dot; 72 pt to the inch, squared, converts inches² to scatter's `s` units.

    Shared by every section-scale slide so they are literally the same geometry rather than
    three copies that agree today. `legend_width` is the reservation for a legend outside the
    axes — pass 0 for a slide that carries none.
    """
    x, y = adata.obsm["spatial"][:, 0], adata.obsm["spatial"][:, 1]
    aspect = (x.max() - x.min()) / (y.max() - y.min())
    plot_w = FIGSIZE[0] - legend_width
    if aspect >= plot_w / FIGSIZE[1]:
        w, h = plot_w, plot_w / aspect
    else:
        w, h = FIGSIZE[1] * aspect, FIGSIZE[1]
    fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(w + legend_width, h))

    pos = ax.get_position()
    area_pt2 = (pos.width * w) * (pos.height * h) * 72 ** 2
    size = float(np.clip(SPATIAL_COVERAGE * area_pt2 / adata.n_obs, 0.5, 6.0))
    return fig, ax, size


def style_tissue_axes(ax):
    """Equal aspect, inverted y and no frame, for an axes drawn in tissue coordinates.

    y is inverted because Xenium global coordinates run downward from the top-left of the
    scan, so a section drawn on default axes is upside down against its own H&E. Applied
    after the data is drawn rather than inside tissue_figure, since inverting an empty axes
    is undone by the first autoscale.
    """
    ax.set_aspect("equal")
    ax.invert_yaxis()
    ax.set_xticks([])
    ax.set_yticks([])
    for spine in ax.spines.values():
        spine.set_visible(False)


def spatial_cell_types(adata, sample, name, labels, title):
    """One slide's figure: the section coloured by cell type rather than cluster id.

    Only the called clusters carry a colour. Everything else is grey and labelled
    unassigned — which on these samples is most of the stroma, and correctly so: the
    marker sets say nothing about it, and coluring it would imply they had.

    Same geometry as the cluster tissue plot (figure shaped to the tissue, marker sized
    from the axes, y inverted), so the two read as the same section.
    """
    x, y = adata.obsm["spatial"][:, 0], adata.obsm["spatial"][:, 1]
    fig, ax, size = tissue_figure(adata)

    cluster = adata.obs[name].astype(str)
    called = cluster.map(labels)
    # Unassigned first and in grey, so the called cells are drawn over it.
    unassigned = called.isna().to_numpy()
    ax.scatter(x[unassigned], y[unassigned], color="0.85", label="unassigned",
               s=size, alpha=1.0, edgecolors="none", rasterized=True)

    for label, color in cell_type_palette(labels).items():
        m = (called == label).to_numpy()
        if m.any():
            ax.scatter(x[m], y[m], color=color, label=label,
                       s=size, alpha=1.0, edgecolors="none", rasterized=True)

    style_tissue_axes(ax)
    ax.legend(loc="center left", bbox_to_anchor=(1.0, 0.5), frameon=False,
              fontsize=7, markerscale=6, handletextpad=0.2, title="cell type",
              title_fontsize=7)

    n_called = int((~unassigned).sum())
    fig.suptitle(f"{sample} · {title} · {n_called:,} of {adata.n_obs:,} cells assigned",
                 fontsize=9, x=0.01, ha="left")
    fig.tight_layout()
    plt.show()
    plt.close(fig)


def spatial_clusters(adata, sample, name):
    """One slide's figure: this sample's cells in tissue coordinates, coloured by cluster.

    The UMAP says which cells group together; only this says whether that group is a
    STRUCTURE. A cluster scattered evenly through the section and a cluster forming
    discrete round bodies are the same picture on a UMAP and different biology here.

    Drawn as bare centroids over white rather than over the morphology or H&E image.
    spatialdata_plot renders those happily — but the tissue's own texture competes with
    the cluster colours at section scale and the result reads as mud, which is the
    opposite of what this slide is for. The image belongs on a slide whose question is
    "what tissue is this", not "where is this cluster".

    Centroids from obsm["spatial"], not the cell_boundaries polygons: at section scale a
    15 µm cell is well under a pixel, so the polygons cost a great deal of render time to
    draw the same dots.

    Figure shape, marker size and the inverted y axis are tissue_figure's and
    style_tissue_axes', shared with every other section-scale slide here; cluster_report
    does all three the same way.
    """
    x, y = adata.obsm["spatial"][:, 0], adata.obsm["spatial"][:, 1]
    fig, ax, size = tissue_figure(adata)

    # Largest cluster first, so small ones are drawn last and land on top. The reverse
    # buries a 500-cell cluster under a 10,000-cell one wherever they overlap — which in
    # tissue is everywhere, since a follicle sits inside stroma rather than beside it.
    labels = adata.obs[name]
    colors = adata.uns[f"{name}_colors"]
    counts = labels.value_counts()
    for level in sorted(labels.cat.categories, key=lambda l: -counts[l]):
        m = (labels == level).to_numpy()
        ax.scatter(x[m], y[m], color=colors[int(level) - 1], label=level,
                   s=size, alpha=1.0, edgecolors="none", rasterized=True)

    style_tissue_axes(ax)

    # Legend rather than on-data labels: a cluster spread across a whole section has its
    # median in the middle of everything else, so the label lands on cells it does not
    # belong to. markerscale lifts the key dots off the plotted size, which is a speck.
    #
    # Handles are reordered numerically before being handed over. Draw order and legend
    # order are separate concerns that matplotlib ties together: the scatters run
    # largest-cluster-first so the small ones land on top, which would otherwise leave
    # the legend reading 1, 4, 2, 7... The reorder keeps both — z-stacking by size, key
    # by number.
    handles, keys = ax.get_legend_handles_labels()
    by_number = sorted(range(len(keys)), key=lambda i: int(keys[i]))
    ax.legend([handles[i] for i in by_number], [keys[i] for i in by_number],
              loc="center left", bbox_to_anchor=(1.0, 0.5), frameon=False,
              fontsize=7, markerscale=6, handletextpad=0.2, title=name,
              title_fontsize=7)

    fig.suptitle(f"{sample} · {adata.n_obs:,} cells · {labels.nunique()} clusters · tissue",
                 fontsize=9, x=0.01, ha="left")
    fig.tight_layout()
    plt.show()
    plt.close(fig)


def stage_representatives(adata):
    """One curated oocyte per developmental stage in this sample, in developmental order.

    The sheet holds every putative oocyte a curator marked — 48 of them in one test crop —
    which is far more than a deck can carry a slide each for. Taking one per stage turns
    that list into a developmental series: the question these slides answer is whether the
    clustering resolves an oocyte at all and from what stage onward, and a second
    primordial follicle does not help answer it.

    The representative is the curator's most confident call for that stage, breaking ties
    on the largest segmented area — the bigger cell of two equally-graded ones is the
    easier read at this magnification. Quality is ranked rather than filtered so a stage
    represented only by a poor cell still gets its slide, with the grade in the caption.

    Both sorts are `kind="stable"`, so two rows agreeing on every key keep their sheet
    order rather than swapping between renders of the same data.
    """
    if CURATED_OOCYTES.empty:
        return []
    present = CURATED_OOCYTES[CURATED_OOCYTES["cell_id"].isin(set(adata.obs_names))]
    if present.empty:
        return []

    unknown_quality = len(OOCYTE_QUALITY_RANK)
    ranked = present.assign(
        _quality=present["Quality"].map(OOCYTE_QUALITY_RANK).fillna(unknown_quality)
    ).sort_values(["_quality", "cell_area"], ascending=[True, False], kind="stable")

    # A stage the order does not name still gets a slide, sorted after the ones it does —
    # a curator adding a label should not have it silently dropped.
    stage_rank = {stage: i for i, stage in enumerate(OOCYTE_STAGE_ORDER)}
    chosen = ranked.groupby("Stage.Labels", sort=False).head(1)
    chosen = chosen.sort_values(
        "Stage.Labels", kind="stable",
        key=lambda col: col.map(lambda s: stage_rank.get(s, len(stage_rank))))
    return chosen.to_dict("records")


def style_scalebar(ax):
    """Give a boxless scale bar a dark stroke, so it reads over whatever it lands on.

    SCALEBAR_PARAMS draws the bar white with no box behind it, which is legible over the
    cell fills but thin against a pale patch of H&E. The stroke is the same trick
    style_on_data_labels uses on the cluster ids: an outline in the opposite tone means the
    mark no longer depends on what is underneath it.

    Applied after the fact because matplotlib-scalebar takes a colour but no path effects.
    The bar and its label are a Rectangle and a Text inside the ScaleBar artist, so both are
    reached through findobj rather than by walking the offsetbox by hand.
    """
    for bar in ax.findobj(ScaleBar):
        for artist in bar.findobj(Text) + bar.findobj(Rectangle):
            artist.set_path_effects(
                [patheffects.withStroke(linewidth=2, foreground="black")])


def color_marker_points(ax, values, colors):
    """Recolour a rendered points panel per marker set, legend included.

    render_points' own `palette` does nothing for points in this version — whatever is
    passed, the drawn colours come out tab10 — so the colours are set on the artist after
    the fact. That is not a style preference: on this panel the default put theca at the
    stroma's own luminance and lost it (see MARKER_TX_COLORS).

    spatialdata_plot draws every point in ONE PathCollection with a per-point colour array,
    rather than one collection per category, so the colours go on in row order — `values` is
    the frame's marker_set column, in the same order it was registered. The empty
    collections beside it are the legend's proxies; the legend has already been built by
    show(), so its handles carry their own colours and are recoloured by label. Run this
    BEFORE legend_below, which rebuilds the legend from those same handles.
    """
    collections = list(ax.collections)
    if not collections:
        return
    drawn = max(collections, key=lambda c: len(c.get_offsets()))
    # Edge as well as face, and the same colour for both. render_points gives each dot an
    # edge in its own colour, so the drawn dot is the marker plus its stroke; clearing the
    # edge instead of recolouring it leaves the face alone and the dots read visibly smaller
    # than they did before — a size change nobody asked for, disguised as a colour change.
    point_colors = [colors[v] for v in values]
    drawn.set_facecolor(point_colors)
    drawn.set_edgecolor(point_colors)

    legend = ax.get_legend()
    if legend is None:
        return
    for handle, text in zip(legend.legend_handles, legend.get_texts()):
        if text.get_text() in colors:
            handle.set_facecolor(colors[text.get_text()])


def legend_below(ax):
    """Move an axes' legend from beside it to a row underneath it.

    spatialdata_plot puts every legend to the RIGHT of its panel, which is fine for one
    panel and unworkable for three: each legend is drawn in the gap the next panel occupies,
    so the labels collide with it and are clipped — on a three-panel zoom the cluster numbers
    vanished entirely and the cell type names ran under the transcript panel.

    Underneath is where the room is, since these panels are square and the slide is wide.
    The legend is rebuilt rather than repositioned because matplotlib's `loc` is fixed at
    construction; handles and text come off the original, so the colours stay whatever
    spatialdata_plot assigned.

    Short keys (cluster ids) go in one row, long ones (cell type names) in two columns —
    seven names at full width would run off both edges of the panel.
    """
    leg = ax.get_legend()
    if leg is None:
        return
    handles = leg.legend_handles
    labels = [t.get_text() for t in leg.get_texts()]
    leg.remove()
    ncol = len(labels) if max((len(l) for l in labels), default=0) <= 4 else 2
    ax.legend(handles, labels, loc="upper center", bbox_to_anchor=(0.5, -0.01),
              frameon=False, fontsize=6, ncol=ncol, handletextpad=0.2,
              columnspacing=0.8, borderpad=0.0)


def zoom_window_centre(adata, record):
    """The (x, y) centre of a curated cell's zoom window, in µm.

    obsm["spatial"] is µm while the `global` frame a crop is taken in is PIXELS, so this is
    the µm half of that pair — the drawing side. oocyte_zoom converts it once for the crop
    and every box here uses it as-is, which is what keeps a box and the window it stands for
    from drifting apart by a scale factor.
    """
    idx = adata.obs_names.get_loc(str(record["cell_id"]))
    return (float(v) for v in adata.obsm["spatial"][idx])


def oocyte_zoom_map(adata, sample, records):
    """One slide's figure: the section with every zoom window boxed, in developmental order.

    The zoom slides that follow are 200 µm windows out of a section a few millimetres
    across, and nothing on them says where. This is the slide that says it, and it says all
    of them at once — which is the part an inset on each zoom cannot do. Whether the stages
    come from one cortical region or from opposite ends of the section is a question about
    the series rather than about any one window, and it is visible here and nowhere else.

    Cells are drawn in one grey rather than by cluster or cell type. The calls have their own
    slides directly above; repeating them here would compete with the boxes for attention on
    a slide whose only question is where.

    Numbered rather than labelled in place: the stage names run to "early transitioning", and
    two windows in the same follicle-rich region would overlap into an unreadable pile. The
```
